angle: When the algorithm flags an autistic candidate's low 'engagement' score for manual review, does the human reviewer overturn the machine's judgment or countersign it — is the flag functioning as a second chance or as a mark that primes the hand that touches it next?
correction_moment: In the employer network's Q3 2024 audit spreadsheet, obtained through a records request to the workforce board, candidates flagged below the engagement threshold were hired at a higher rate than candidates who narrowly cleared it and were never seen by a human at all — the flag Zen came to expose as a mark had, in at least one quarter's data, functioned as a rescue.
cross_cite: Against the archival position that the correct response to a biased instrument is a complete, unedited record of every judgment it renders, this piece tests whether repair is even a coherent goal when the last three systems Zen examined showed the reviewing hand re-signing the machine's error anyway — documentation may be all that survives contact with the pipeline, and Zen goes in refusing to accept that.
opening_scene: An engagement score is a measurement of how closely you resemble the people who were hired before the camera arrived.
resisting_example: An autistic recruiter inside the same employer network formally requested that her own promotion interview be machine-scored rather than panel-judged, on the record with HR, because the algorithm publishes its threshold and a human panel reading her flat affect never has — she defends the tool from inside the exact community it flags.
seed_sentence: An engagement score is a measurement of how closely you resemble the people who were hired before the camera arrived.
